notes.meaning: Micah received a message directly from the LORD during the rules of three kings of Judah: Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. He came from a small country town called Moresheth, but God gave him visions about the capital cities of Samaria and Jerusalem. Samaria was the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and Jerusalem was the capital of the southern kingdom of Judah. Because both nations turned away from God, the prophet had to announce God's coming judgment against both of them.

The prophet calls out to all the nations and the entire earth to stop and listen. God is stepping forward as a witness in a courtroom against His own rebellious people. He speaks with supreme authority from His holy dwelling place. Since the people ignored God's gentle warnings, He now calls the whole world to watch His justice take place.

The LORD is pictured as leaving His heavenly home to come down to the earth as a judge. When He arrives, He will march across the high hilltops and strong mountain forts. The people trusted in their high walled cities and mountain shrines for safety, but nothing can stop God when He comes to correct evil.

Poetic pictures of an earthquake and a raging storm show the awesome power of God's presence. Strong mountains will melt away like soft wax near a flame, and deep valleys will crack wide open like water rushing down a steep hill. These word pictures warn that neither the highest rulers nor the lowest common people can protect themselves from God's holy anger.

All this destruction comes because God's covenant people fell into deep rebellion and sin. The rot of the whole northern nation came straight from its capital city, Samaria, where false worship was set up by its kings. In the same way, the unlawful worship sites that polluted the southern land came from the leaders in Jerusalem.

God announces that the great city of Samaria will be turned into a pile of loose field stones. Its ruins will become an open hillside where farmers plant rows of grapevines. Invaders will tear down its stone buildings, roll the rubble down into the valley below, and completely strip away its foundations.

All the carved statues and idols that Samaria bowed down to will be smashed to pieces or burned. The people treated their wealth like the earnings of a prostitute, believing their false gods had blessed them with riches for their worship. Invading armies will plunder that stolen treasure and carry it off to their own idol temples, showing how empty and worthless it all was.

Micah is so overwhelmed by the coming ruin that he weeps aloud like a wild animal. He walks around without shoes and without his outer cloak, acting out the terrible grief and public shame of prisoners of war being led away. His cries of pain sound like the mournful howling of jackals and the screeching of ostriches in the night.

The spiritual disease and deadly strike against Samaria cannot be healed, because the time for turning back has passed. Worst of all, this invading wave of destruction will not stop with the northern kingdom; it will push right into Judah. The enemy army will march all the way up to the city gates of Jerusalem itself.

The people are warned not to let their enemies in the Philistine city of Gath hear about their disaster, so those enemies cannot mock them. At the same time, in the Jewish town of Beth-leaphrah, which means 'House of Dust,' the people are told to roll on the ground in deep sorrow. The prophet uses the meaning of the town's name to show that their proud homes are turning into plain dirt.

The residents of Shaphir, a name that means 'pleasant' or 'beautiful,' will be stripped of their fine clothes and marched away into captivity in total dishonor. The people of Zaanan, whose name sounds like 'come out,' will be too terrified to step outside their city walls. The nearby town of Beth-ezel is weeping in ruin, unable to offer any shelter or help to its neighbors.

The people of Maroth, a name that means 'bitterness,' waited anxiously for relief and good news, but their hopes were crushed. Instead of peace, the LORD sent bitter trouble rolling through their land. That disaster swept past their villages and moved all the way to the front gate of Jerusalem.

The citizens of the chariot city of Lachish are told to hitch their fastest horses and run for their lives. Lachish was the first town in Judah to welcome the idol worship of the northern kingdom, and from there the spiritual rot spread directly into Jerusalem. Because Lachish led the way into rebellion against God, it must be among the first to suffer the invasion.

Judah must now say goodbye to the border town of Moresheth-gath, sending it away like a bride given over to an enemy master. Meanwhile, the town of Achzib, whose name means 'deceitful,' will fail the kings of Israel just like a stream that runs completely dry in the summer heat. Human alliances and local fortresses will prove to be false hopes that collapse in the day of trouble.

God warns the town of Mareshah, whose name sounds like 'inheritance,' that He will hand it over to a new heir—the invading conqueror who will take total possession of it. Judah's royal leaders and nobles, who were once the glory of the nation, will have to run and hide in the caves of Adullam, just as David did when he was an outlaw on the run.

The people of Judah are told to shave their heads completely bald as a public sign of unbearable grief for the precious children they loved and spoiled. They should make their heads as bare as a vulture, because enemy armies are going to round up their sons and daughters and march them away into exile. All earthly pride and luxury end in tears when people wander away from the living God.
